meta.note: Plain-language explanations for readers who are new to the terms. They are summaries, not the legal definitions: the instrument named under 'See' governs.

terms.def: A promise to pay or perform for a borrower if the borrower defaults. The guarantor is the surety, the borrower the principal debtor and the lender the creditor (Contract Act s. 126).
A guarantee that covers a series of transactions, such as a running cash-credit account. The surety can revoke it for future transactions by notice; past liability survives (ss. 129-130).
The guarantor is released, fully or partly, if the lender changes the loan terms, gives the borrower time, releases the borrower or loses security without the guarantor's consent (ss. 133-141).
A promise to make good a loss suffered by the other party, whether caused by the promisor or anyone else (s. 124).
Security over goods or other movables by handing them over to the lender. The lender may sell them after reasonable notice if the borrower defaults (ss. 172, 176).
A charge over movable property, present or future, without handing it over to the lender; it includes a floating charge (SARFAESI s. 2(1)(n)). Common for vehicle, equipment and stock loans.
A bank's right to keep goods or securities of a customer in its hands as security for the customer's general balance, unless agreed otherwise (s. 171).
Security over land or buildings by transferring an interest in the property to the lender (TPA s. 58). There are six kinds, including simple, English and by deposit of title-deeds.
A mortgage made by handing over the title documents of a property, with intent to create security, in a notified town. It needs no registered deed (TPA s. 58(f)).
Security over immovable property that does not amount to a mortgage, created by agreement or by law. The rules for simple mortgages apply to it (TPA s. 100).
The borrower's right to pay off a mortgage and get back the title deeds and the property (TPA s. 60).
A court decree that ends the borrower's right to redeem a mortgage. In everyday banking the word also means early repayment of a loan, which is a different thing.

The transfer of an unsecured debt or receivable by a signed written instrument. Until the debtor gets express notice, its payments to the original creditor remain valid (TPA ss. 130-131). Secured loans are transferred with their security under other rules.
Under SARFAESI, a bank, notified financial institution, asset reconstruction company or debenture trustee holding a security interest. Only secured creditors can use SARFAESI.
Any right, title or interest in property created for a secured creditor, including a mortgage, charge, hypothecation or assignment (SARFAESI s. 2(1)(zf)).
The SARFAESI notice asking a defaulting borrower whose account is an NPA to pay in full within 60 days, before the lender can take possession.
The step after the 60-day demand notice: the lender takes possession of the secured asset, takes over the business or asks the borrower's debtors to pay it directly.

The Central Registry of Securitisation Asset Reconstruction and Security Interest of India, where lenders record security interests. A secured creditor cannot enforce under SARFAESI unless its security is registered there (s. 26D).

The tribunal that hears recovery cases of banks and notified financial institutions above the RDB Act threshold (Rs 10 lakh in the Act, or another amount the Central Government notifies) and borrowers' challenges to SARFAESI action.
The appeal tribunal above the DRT. A borrower appealing must usually deposit 50% of the debt, which can be reduced to 25%.
The certificate the DRT issues for the amount due. The Recovery Officer then recovers it by attachment and sale, arrest, or a receiver (RDB s. 25).
A written, signed admission of liability by the borrower or guarantor before limitation expires. It starts a fresh limitation period (Limitation Act s. 18).
The time within which a lender must sue: generally three years for a loan, twelve years to enforce a mortgage (Limitation Act Schedule).
A tax on documents such as loan agreements, mortgages and guarantees. Under-stamped documents cannot be used as evidence until duty and penalty are paid (Stamp Act s. 35).
When an unstamped or under-stamped document is produced before a court or officer, it is kept back until the proper duty and penalty are paid (Stamp Act s. 33).

Documents that create or transfer rights of Rs 100 or more in immovable property must be registered with the Sub-Registrar within four months, or they do not affect the property (Registration Act ss. 17, 23, 49).
The offence when a cheque given for a debt is returned unpaid for lack of funds and the drawer does not pay within 15 days of a demand notice.
The offence when an ECS, NACH or other electronic debit for a debt fails for lack of funds and the payer does not pay within 15 days of a demand notice.
The certificate required to put an electronic record, such as an e-signed agreement or system statement, in evidence. It is signed by the person in charge of the system and an expert (BSA s. 63(4)).
A copy of an entry in a bank's books, certified by an authorised officer, which courts accept as evidence of the entry (Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 2026 s. 5).

Recovery methods that State laws ban, such as threats, violence, following the borrower, visiting the home or workplace to pressure, or seizing documents (for example Tamil Nadu Act 40 of 2025 s. 20).
A company registered with RBI that collects credit data from lenders and supplies credit reports. Every lender must be a member of at least one (CICRA s. 15).
A seller who has not been paid in full. He keeps a lien on the goods in his possession and can stop them in transit, even after ownership has passed (Sale of Goods Act ss. 45-47).
Getting a broken contract performed by someone else and recovering the cost from the party in breach, after 30 days' notice (Specific Relief Act s. 20).
A shortfall in the quality or manner of a service, including banking and lending, that a consumer can complain about to a consumer commission (CPA s. 2(11)).
